idiom_name: public trait plus private[package] implementation, MiMa-checked
implementation_notes: Scala expresses the split with qualified private access: a public trait or abstract class is the contract, the implementation sits in a private[mypackage] class constructed by a companion factory, and because the JVM links by name against class files, changing private members never forces consumers to recompile. Two caveats shape the method - qualified private is compile-time only (the JVM and reflection still see those members as public), and binary compatibility is enforced as a build gate with MiMa, which compares two releases' class files and fails on signatures that would break existing clients. Inline definitions sharpen it further: reading a private or qualified-private member from an inline def makes the compiler emit accessors that become part of the binary API, which is what SIP-52's @publicInBinary exists to make explicit.
pitfalls: private[pkg] is erased to public in bytecode, so Java callers and reflection ignore it, and packages are open in Scala: a hard boundary needs JPMS exports or a separate artifact.
Because the qualifier is compile-time, MiMa still reports package-private removals as binary incompatibilities - plan them, or keep a @publicInBinary or private[C] shim for the removed member.

Inline code over non-public members generates accessors whose names are implementation details but whose presence is a binary contract; changing the visibility later breaks consumers compiled against the accessor.
